title: Hacker CLI Gym: 100 Foundational Linux Commands

lessons.title: Know where you are
lessons.about: pwd prints the absolute path of the shell's current working directory. Use it before a relative-path operation when location is uncertain.
breakdown: The result anchors every relative path that follows.
lessons.task: Print the absolute path of this disposable practice workspace.
hints: The topic command prints the current working directory.
lessons.completion: Orient first. A correct command in the wrong directory can still produce the wrong result.

lessons.title: List visible and hidden entries
lessons.about: ls lists directory entries. -a includes dotfiles and -1 prints one name per line, which makes the result easier to inspect or pipe.
breakdown: -a includes names beginning with a dot.
-1 uses one output line per entry.
lessons.task: List every entry in the workspace, including hidden entries, one name per line.
hints: Combine the all and one-entry-per-line options.
lessons.completion: A plain ls can hide operationally important dotfiles. Ask for the view the task actually requires.

lessons.title: Change directory deliberately
lessons.about: cd is a shell builtin that changes the current working directory. This rep combines it with pwd so the changed location is observable in one shell execution.
breakdown: cd reports changes location only if it succeeds.
&& runs pwd after a successful change.
lessons.task: Change into the reports directory and print the resulting absolute path.
hints: Use && to verify the change only after cd succeeds.

checks.description: The reports directory became the working directory.

lessons.completion: cd changes shell state; it normally prints nothing. Pair navigation with pwd when you need explicit confirmation.

lessons.title: Extract the final path component
lessons.about: basename removes leading directory components from a path string. It does not require the named path to exist.
breakdown: daily.txt is the final path component.
lessons.task: Print only the filename component of projects/alpha/notes.md.
hints: Pass the complete relative path to basename.
lessons.completion: basename transforms a path string; it does not inspect or validate the filesystem object.

lessons.title: Extract the directory portion
lessons.about: dirname removes the final component from a path string and prints the directory portion.
breakdown: daily.txt is removed from the string.
The remaining directory expression is printed.
lessons.task: Print only the directory portion of projects/alpha/notes.md.
hints: dirname complements basename.
lessons.completion: dirname is string processing. Combine it with realpath when canonical filesystem resolution matters.

lessons.title: Resolve a canonical absolute path
lessons.about: realpath resolves a path to a canonical absolute form, removing relative components and following symbolic links by default.
breakdown: notes.txt begins as a relative path.
realpath emits its resolved absolute form.
lessons.task: Resolve notes.txt to its absolute canonical path.
hints: Pass the relative filename to realpath.

checks.description: The canonical notes.txt path was printed.

lessons.completion: Canonicalization can follow links and change the visible path. Preserve the original path separately when that distinction matters.

lessons.title: Locate an executable on PATH
lessons.about: which searches PATH for an executable name. It is useful for a quick external-command location, but shell builtins and aliases require type or command -V.
breakdown: PATH directories are searched in order.
The first matching executable path is printed.
lessons.task: Print the executable path selected for grep.
hints: Give which the executable name, not a full path.

checks.description: The selected path ends with grep.

lessons.completion: which answers a PATH question. Use type when shell functions, aliases, and builtins are also possible.

lessons.title: Find command-related paths
lessons.about: whereis searches standard locations for a command's binary, source, and manual-page files. Its result can contain several paths.
breakdown: The labeled result may include a binary and documentation.
lessons.task: Use whereis to locate files associated with bash.
hints: Pass the command name to whereis.

checks.description: The result was labeled for bash.

lessons.completion: whereis uses known location databases, not an unrestricted filesystem walk. Use find for a scoped live search.

lessons.title: Ask Bash how a name resolves
lessons.about: type is a Bash builtin that explains whether a name resolves to an alias, function, builtin, keyword, or executable.
breakdown: cd is looked up using Bash's own resolution rules.
The result identifies it as a builtin.
lessons.task: Ask Bash how the name cd resolves.
hints: Use the shell builtin named in the topic.

checks.description: cd was identified as a shell builtin.

lessons.completion: type is more complete than which for understanding what Bash will actually execute.

lessons.title: Open local command documentation
lessons.about: man displays local manual pages. This noninteractive rep checks the help surface; in a normal terminal, man ls opens the complete page in a pager.
breakdown: --help prints man usage without opening a pager.
lessons.task: Print the first line of man's own help output.
hints: Request --help, then limit the result to one line.

checks.description: A man help line was printed.

lessons.completion: Manual pages are local, version-matched references. Search inside a page with /pattern and leave the pager with q.

lessons.title: Create a nested directory tree
lessons.about: mkdir creates directories. -p creates missing parents and treats an existing requested directory as success.
breakdown: The final screenshots directory is created below it.
lessons.task: Create reports/daily in one command.
hints: Use the parent-creation option.
lessons.completion: mkdir -p is script-friendly, but a typo can still create the wrong tree. Verify the path.

lessons.title: Remove an empty directory
lessons.about: rmdir removes empty directories only. That narrow behavior is safer than recursive removal when emptiness is a required precondition.
breakdown: A successful removal normally prints nothing.
lessons.task: Remove the empty directory named retired.
hints: The directory is empty, so recursive rm is unnecessary.

checks.description: The retired directory no longer exists.

lessons.completion: rmdir refuses nonempty directories. That refusal is useful evidence that the scope is broader than expected.

lessons.title: Create an empty marker file
lessons.about: touch creates a missing file or updates timestamps on an existing one. It does not guarantee that an existing file is empty.
lessons.task: Create an empty file named complete.flag.
hints: Pass the new filename to touch.
lessons.completion: touch is also a timestamp tool. Inspect before assuming it created a new empty file.

lessons.title: Copy without changing the source
lessons.about: cp creates a destination from a source. A plain copy can overwrite an existing path, so verify both names first.
lessons.task: Copy briefing.txt to briefing.backup.
hints: Source comes before destination.
lessons.completion: Copying preserves the source path. Metadata preservation requires explicit options such as -a or -p.

lessons.title: Rename a file
lessons.about: mv moves or renames a path. Within one filesystem, a rename usually changes directory metadata rather than copying file bytes.
lessons.task: Rename report.draft to report.final.
hints: Use the old path first and new path second.
lessons.completion: mv can overwrite a destination. Use -i or -n when accidental replacement is a concern.

lessons.title: Remove one disposable file
lessons.about: rm unlinks files. This rep is constrained to a synthetic temporary workspace that is discarded after completion.
breakdown: Only the named file is removed.
No recursive or force option is needed.
lessons.task: Remove trash.txt and nothing else.
hints: Name the one disposable file directly.
lessons.completion: rm normally has no undo. Narrow the target, avoid unnecessary -r/-f, and verify what must remain.

lessons.title: Create a hard link
lessons.about: ln creates a hard link by default. Both directory entries refer to the same inode rather than storing two independent copies.
breakdown: second-name.txt becomes another name for that inode.
lessons.task: Create hardlink.txt as a hard link to source.txt.
hints: Do not add -s; this rep asks for a hard link.

checks.description: Both names reference the same inode.

lessons.completion: Hard links share content and inode metadata. Removing one name does not remove the inode while another hard link remains.

lessons.title: Inspect a symbolic-link target
lessons.about: readlink prints the target stored in a symbolic link. The stored target may itself be relative and may not exist.
breakdown: readlink prints its stored target string.
lessons.task: Create latest.log pointing to logs/app.log, then print the stored target.
hints: Create a symbolic link with ln -s, then inspect it.

checks.description: The stored relative target was printed.

lessons.completion: readlink reports the link's stored target; realpath resolves the resulting path through the filesystem.

lessons.title: Identify content type from bytes
lessons.about: file examines content signatures and heuristics rather than trusting only a filename extension.
breakdown: The file's bytes drive the description.
lessons.task: Ask file to identify sample.txt without printing its filename.
hints: Use brief mode with -b.

checks.description: The data was identified as text.

lessons.completion: file is a clue, not a security verdict. Treat its label as an observation to validate when stakes are higher.

lessons.title: Read exact file metadata
lessons.about: stat reports filesystem metadata. GNU stat -c accepts a format string so scripts can request only the needed field.
lessons.task: Print only the byte size of bytes.txt.
hints: Use GNU stat format token %s.
lessons.completion: Metadata formats differ across Unix families. This rep deliberately targets GNU stat as found on Linux.

lessons.title: Print a short text file
lessons.about: cat writes file bytes to standard output. It is convenient for small known text files and as a pipeline source.
breakdown: Its content is sent to stdout.
lessons.task: Print all lines from briefing.txt.
hints: Pass the filename to cat.
lessons.completion: Use less for long output and avoid sending unknown binary data directly to a terminal.

lessons.title: Page through long text
lessons.about: less is an interactive pager with search and navigation. -F exits when the content fits and -X avoids clearing the terminal, making this rep noninteractive.
breakdown: -F quits when one screen is enough.
lessons.task: Display note.txt through less and let it exit because the file is short.
hints: Combine -F and -X for this short noninteractive rep.

files.note.txt:
search with /pattern
next match with n
quit with q

checks.description: The pager emitted the note content.

lessons.completion: In a real interactive page, use /pattern to search, n for the next match, and q to quit.

lessons.title: Read the beginning
lessons.about: head prints the beginning of a file or stream. -n sets an exact line count.
lessons.task: Print only the first three lines of events.txt.
hints: Use -n with a value of 3.

checks.description: The first three events were printed.

lessons.completion: head is ideal for quickly learning a file's header and record shape.

lessons.title: Read the end
lessons.about: tail prints the end of a file or stream. -n chooses the count; -f follows a growing file interactively.
lessons.task: Print only the final two lines of events.txt.
hints: Use tail with -n 2.

checks.description: The final two events were printed.

lessons.completion: tail -f is useful for live logs, but always stop the follower cleanly with Ctrl-C.

lessons.title: Number text lines
lessons.about: nl numbers lines with configurable treatment of blank lines. Its default output includes padded line numbers and a tab.
lessons.task: Number every line in note.txt, including the blank line.
hints: Use body-numbering style a to number all lines.

checks.description: The blank line received line number 2.

lessons.completion: nl has its own rules for logical pages and blank lines. Use cat -n when its simpler numbering behavior is what you need.

lessons.title: Reverse records by line
lessons.about: tac prints file lines from last to first. Its name is cat reversed, but it reverses record order rather than characters.
breakdown: The final input line is printed first.
Characters inside each line keep their order.
lessons.task: Print priorities.txt from its final line to its first.
hints: Pass the filename directly to tac.
lessons.completion: tac is a GNU/Linux utility; it reverses records, not bytes or words.

lessons.title: Extract printable sequences
lessons.about: strings scans data for printable character sequences. It is useful for triage, but extracted text lacks the structure and provenance of a parser.
breakdown: Printable runs meeting the minimum length are emitted.
lessons.task: Extract printable strings from blob.bin.
hints: No option is required for the supplied blob.

checks.description: The synthetic secret string was recovered.

lessons.completion: strings reveals printable runs, not necessarily meaningful fields. Validate findings with format-aware tools.

lessons.title: Inspect exact byte values
lessons.about: od displays file bytes in selected numeric forms. -An removes offsets and -t x1 requests one-byte hexadecimal values.
breakdown: x1 selects hexadecimal one byte at a time.
lessons.task: Print bytes.txt as one-byte hexadecimal values without offsets.
hints: Combine -An with -t x1.

checks.description: The exact four byte values were printed.

lessons.completion: Byte views expose line endings, encodings, and hidden delimiters that rendered text can conceal.

lessons.title: Create a plain hexadecimal dump
lessons.about: xxd converts bytes to hexadecimal and can reverse a compatible dump. -p selects a plain continuous hex form.
breakdown: Each byte becomes two hex digits.
lessons.task: Print bytes.txt as plain hexadecimal.
hints: Use xxd plain mode.

checks.description: The plain hex bytes were printed.

lessons.completion: xxd -r reverses a compatible dump. A hex representation is evidence of bytes, not an interpretation of their format.

lessons.title: Count lines
lessons.about: wc reports lines, words, and byte or character counts. -l asks specifically for lines.
breakdown: Naming a file includes its name in output.
lessons.task: Count the lines in requests.txt and retain the filename label.
hints: Use the line-count option.

checks.description: wc reported five lines for requests.txt.

lessons.completion: In a pipeline, wc -l counts records that survive the preceding filters.

lessons.title: Select delimited fields
lessons.about: cut selects fields when input has a dependable simple delimiter. -d names the delimiter and -f chooses fields.
lessons.task: accounts.txt uses colons. Print only the username in field 2.
hints: Set colon as delimiter and select field 2.
lessons.completion: cut does not understand quoted CSV. Use a format-aware parser when delimiters can appear inside fields.

lessons.title: Merge files line by line
lessons.about: paste combines corresponding lines from input files. -d selects the output delimiter.
breakdown: Line 1 from each file is joined.
lessons.task: Combine hosts.txt and states.txt line by line with a comma.
hints: Use comma as paste's delimiter.

checks.description: Each host was paired with its state.

lessons.completion: paste pairs by line position. Validate row counts first when accidental misalignment would matter.

lessons.title: Keep matching records
lessons.about: grep searches text and prints matching lines. -F is a useful choice when the pattern must be treated literally.
lessons.task: Print every service.log line containing DENIED.
hints: Give grep the pattern and filename.

files.service.log:
08:00 ALLOWED alice
08:02 DENIED bob
08:04 ALLOWED carol
08:05 DENIED dave

checks.description: Only the DENIED records were printed.

lessons.completion: Start literal, then add regular-expression power only when the task needs it.

lessons.title: Transform a text stream
lessons.about: sed applies editing expressions to a stream. Without -i, transformed output goes to stdout and the source remains unchanged.
breakdown: g replaces all matches on each line.
lessons.task: Print config.txt with every DEBUG changed to INFO, without editing the file.
hints: Use a global substitution and omit -i.
lessons.completion: Preview stream output before an in-place edit. That small habit prevents many accidental file changes.

lessons.title: Process records and fields
lessons.about: awk splits input into records and fields, then applies a small program. It handles conditional selection, formatting, and aggregation.
lessons.task: Print asset name, colon-space, and status from inventory.csv fields 1 and 3.
hints: Set comma as -F and concatenate fields 1 and 3.

checks.description: Each asset and status was formatted correctly.
checks.expected:
web-01: online
db-01: maintenance
api-02: offline

lessons.completion: awk is a record-processing language. Build and inspect small stages before compressing complex logic.

lessons.title: Translate characters
lessons.about: tr translates or deletes characters from standard input. It operates character by character rather than on words or fields.
breakdown: Character classes describe lower and upper case.
lessons.task: Print message.txt with lowercase letters converted to uppercase.
hints: Redirect the file into tr and use character classes.

checks.description: The message was converted to uppercase.

lessons.completion: tr is ideal for character-level mappings. Use sed or awk when context and fields matter.

lessons.title: Order records
lessons.about: sort orders lines. Its default is lexical; use -n when numeric value rather than string order is intended.
breakdown: Every line becomes a sort record.
The source file is not edited.
lessons.task: Print hosts.txt in ascending lexical order.
hints: Pass the filename to sort.
lessons.completion: Sorting output does not sort the source file. Redirect to a new file and verify before replacing data.

lessons.title: Collapse adjacent duplicates
lessons.about: uniq compares neighboring lines. Sort first when equal values may be separated in the original input.
lessons.task: Print each distinct color once in ascending order.
hints: Pipe sorted input into uniq.

checks.description: Each color was printed once in order.

lessons.completion: uniq is adjacency-based. sort | uniq is the standard pattern for unordered text values.

lessons.title: Align delimited text for people
lessons.about: column formats input into aligned columns. It is a display tool; do not parse its padded output as a stable data format.
lessons.task: Format people.csv as an aligned table using comma as the separator.
hints: Combine table mode with comma separator.
lessons.completion: column improves human readability. Preserve CSV, TSV, or JSON for machine consumption.

lessons.title: Reflow paragraph text
lessons.about: fmt reflows paragraphs to a target width. It is useful for prose, not structured records where line boundaries carry meaning.
lessons.example_output:
This is a short line
that wraps cleanly.
breakdown: Words are reflowed without editing the file.
lessons.task: Reflow paragraph.txt to a width of 24 columns.
hints: Use -w to choose the target width.

files.paragraph.txt: Linux commands become easier when each pipeline stage has one clear responsibility.

checks.expected: Linux commands become easier when each pipeline stage has one clear responsibility.

lessons.completion: fmt changes presentation line breaks. Never use it on logs or formats where a line is a record.

lessons.title: Print a simple string
lessons.about: echo prints arguments separated by spaces. Option and escape behavior can vary, so use printf for strict portable formatting.
breakdown: Quotes keep the words as one shell argument.
lessons.task: Print the exact text practical linux.
hints: Quote the two-word string.
lessons.completion: echo is convenient for simple messages. Prefer printf when escapes, leading dashes, or exact formatting matter.

lessons.title: Format output predictably
lessons.about: printf applies a format string to values and does not add a newline unless the format requests one.
breakdown: %s formats one string at a time.
The format repeats for remaining values.
lessons.task: Print red, green, and blue on separate lines with one printf command.
hints: Use %s followed by a newline escape.

checks.description: Each color was printed on its own line.

lessons.completion: Treat the format string as data you control. Do not use untrusted text as the printf format.

lessons.title: See and save one stream
lessons.about: tee copies standard input to standard output and one or more files. It is useful when a pipeline result must remain visible and be saved.
breakdown: tee writes result.txt and passes the same text onward.
lessons.task: Print ready and save the same line in status.txt.
hints: Pipe printf into tee and name the output file.
lessons.completion: tee is not an audit guarantee; later stages can still fail. Preserve exit status and verification when the result matters.

lessons.title: Build argument lists from input
lessons.about: xargs converts input items into command arguments. Delimiters and filenames with spaces require deliberate handling such as NUL-delimited input.
breakdown: -n 1 invokes echo with one item at a time.
lessons.task: Pass red, green, and blue to echo one item per invocation.
hints: Use -n 1 so each command receives one value.

checks.description: Each color was echoed on its own line.

lessons.completion: Use find -print0 with xargs -0 for arbitrary filenames. Whitespace-delimited input is not filename-safe.

lessons.title: Show line-oriented differences
lessons.about: diff compares files line by line. Unified format (-u) provides context and is widely used in reviews and patches.
breakdown: Exit status 1 means files differ, not that diff crashed.
lessons.task: Print a unified comparison of old.txt and new.txt.
hints: Use unified output with -u.

checks.description: The removed alpha line was shown.
The added beta line was shown.

lessons.completion: diff exit 1 means a difference was found. Always interpret a command's documented exit-status contract.

lessons.title: Compare files byte for byte
lessons.about: cmp compares two files byte by byte. -s suppresses output so the exit status alone reports equality.
breakdown: Exit 0 means the byte sequences match.
lessons.task: Silently verify that first.txt and second.txt contain identical bytes.
hints: Use cmp silent mode.
lessons.completion: cmp proves equality of the observed bytes, not that the files are safe, trusted, or correctly named.

lessons.title: Compare sorted sets of lines
lessons.about: comm compares two sorted files in three columns: unique to first, unique to second, and common to both.
lessons.task: Print only lines common to allowed.txt and observed.txt.
hints: Both inputs are already sorted; suppress columns 1 and 2.
lessons.completion: comm assumes sorted inputs under the same locale. Violating that precondition can silently mislead.

lessons.title: Join records by a key
lessons.about: join combines lines from sorted files when a selected key matches. It is a text-file analogue of a relational join.
breakdown: The first field is the default join key.
lessons.task: Join users.csv and roles.csv by their first comma-delimited field.
hints: Both files are sorted by field 1, so the default key works.

checks.description: Every user was joined to a role.

lessons.completion: join expects sorted keys. Use a format-aware data tool when quoting, escaping, or complex joins matter.

lessons.title: Split a file into fixed-size chunks
lessons.about: split divides input into output files by line count or byte size. Output names use a supplied prefix plus generated suffixes.
breakdown: -l 2 places two lines in each part.
lessons.task: Split events.txt into two-line files with prefix part-.
hints: Use -l 2 and provide an output prefix.

checks.description: part-aa contains the first two events.

lessons.completion: Record the split rule and naming pattern so the parts can be reassembled and verified correctly.

lessons.title: Split at a content position
lessons.about: csplit divides a file at line numbers or matching contexts. Unlike split, boundaries can follow content structure.
breakdown: 3 starts the second output at line 3.
lessons.task: Split sections.txt before line 3 without printing byte counts.
hints: Use silent mode and the line number 3.
lessons.completion: csplit boundaries are structural assumptions. Inspect the resulting parts before treating them as complete records.

lessons.title: Set private permission bits
lessons.about: chmod changes POSIX mode bits. Numeric 600 grants owner read/write and no group or other permissions.
breakdown: Both zeros remove group and other mode permissions.
lessons.task: Set secret.txt to mode 600.
hints: Pass numeric mode 600 before the filename.
lessons.completion: Mode bits are one layer. Ownership, ACLs, elevated users, and directory permissions also affect access.

lessons.title: Apply owner metadata by reference
lessons.about: chown changes file ownership. --reference copies owner and group metadata from a known file without hard-coding an account name.
lessons.task: Apply reference.txt ownership to target.txt.
hints: Use GNU chown's --reference option.
lessons.completion: Changing ownership can require privilege when the requested owner differs. This rep remains within the current synthetic owner.

lessons.title: Apply group metadata by reference
lessons.about: chgrp changes a file's group. --reference copies the group from another file and avoids embedding a local group name.
lessons.task: Apply reference.txt group ownership to target.txt.
hints: Use the --reference option.
lessons.completion: Group membership and directory inheritance determine whether a group assignment produces the intended effective access.

lessons.title: Control default creation permissions
lessons.about: umask removes permission bits from newly created files and directories. It affects future creation in the current shell.
breakdown: 077 masks all group and other bits.
The following file is created with mode 600 under normal base permissions.
lessons.task: Set umask 077 and create private.txt in the same shell command.
hints: Set the mask, then use && before touch.
lessons.completion: umask subtracts permissions from creation defaults; it does not add bits or retroactively change existing paths.

lessons.title: Inspect numeric identity context
lessons.about: id reports user and group identity. -u emits only the effective numeric user ID.
breakdown: The result is numeric and environment-specific.
lessons.task: Print only your effective numeric user ID.
hints: Use id's user-only option.

checks.description: A numeric user ID was printed.

lessons.completion: Names are labels resolved through identity databases. Authorization decisions ultimately use numeric IDs and groups.

lessons.title: Print the effective username
lessons.about: whoami prints the name associated with the effective user ID. It is equivalent to id -un on common Linux systems.
lessons.task: Print your effective username.
hints: The topic command takes no argument.
lessons.completion: whoami is a quick identity check. Use id for the complete user and group context.

lessons.title: List group memberships
lessons.about: groups prints the group names associated with a user. With no argument it reports the current process identity context.
breakdown: One or more group names are printed.
lessons.task: Print the group memberships active for your current identity.
hints: Run groups with no username.

checks.description: At least one group was printed.

lessons.completion: A group list is context, not proof of access. Directory traversal, ACLs, and mode bits still determine effective filesystem access.

lessons.title: Query configured identity databases
lessons.about: getent queries databases configured through the Name Service Switch, including local files and network identity sources.
lessons.task: Query the passwd database for root and print only its username field.
hints: Query passwd, then cut the first colon-delimited field.

checks.description: The resolved username root was printed.

lessons.completion: getent follows configured resolution policy. Reading /etc/passwd alone can miss directory-backed identities.

lessons.title: Inspect logged-in usernames
lessons.about: users prints usernames recorded as currently logged in. Minimal containers and some VM sessions may have no utmp records, so empty output can be legitimate.
breakdown: Login records are read from the system session database.
Repeated names can represent multiple sessions.
lessons.task: Run users and observe the current system's login-record result.
hints: No arguments are required; empty output is possible in a container.
lessons.completion: Empty users output does not prove nobody is active; session accounting depends on how the environment records logins.

lessons.title: Inspect login session records
lessons.about: who prints detailed login records such as user, terminal, and login time. Container environments often have no such records.
breakdown: The system session database is queried.
Each record describes a logged-in session.
lessons.task: Run who and observe the login records available in this environment.
hints: Run the command without options; no records is a valid observation.
lessons.completion: Session accounting is one evidence source. Processes, remote access logs, and orchestration context may tell a different part of the story.

lessons.title: Take a process snapshot
lessons.about: ps reports a point-in-time process snapshot. Explicit columns make the output easier to reason about than relying on defaults.
lessons.task: Print PID and command name for process 1 without headers.
hints: Use -p 1 and an explicit -o format.
lessons.completion: ps is a snapshot. Processes can exit, fork, or change state immediately after observation.

lessons.title: Capture a batch process overview
lessons.about: top is normally interactive. -b enables batch output and -n 1 captures one refresh suitable for a file or pipeline.
lessons.task: Capture the first five lines of one batch-mode top sample.
hints: Use batch mode, one iteration, and head.
lessons.completion: One top sample is not a performance conclusion. Compare multiple observations and the workload context.

lessons.title: Find processes by name or command line
lessons.about: pgrep searches the process table. -a prints matching PIDs with command lines and -f matches the full command line.
breakdown: -f broadens matching to full command lines.
-a preserves visible context for each PID.
lessons.task: Find the running Hacker CLI Gym process by matching its full command line and print its PID plus command line.
hints: Combine -a and -f with the pattern hacker-cli-gym.

checks.description: At least one Hacker CLI Gym process context was printed.

lessons.completion: A name match is a candidate set, not authorization to signal every result. Verify PID, owner, arguments, and role first.

lessons.title: Resolve a signal name safely
lessons.about: kill sends signals to processes, while kill -l can list or translate signal names without signaling anything. This rep uses the safe translation form.
breakdown: TERM maps to the standard termination signal number.
lessons.task: Translate the signal name TERM to its number without signaling a process.
hints: Use kill's list/translate option.
lessons.completion: Prefer TERM before KILL so a process can clean up. Confirm the exact PID and ownership before signaling.

lessons.title: Run independently of terminal hangup
lessons.about: nohup changes hangup-signal handling for a command. Redirect output explicitly so its destination is predictable.
breakdown: > sends stdout to a declared file.
lessons.task: Use nohup to run printf and write ready to nohup-result.txt.
hints: Put printf after nohup and redirect stdout.
lessons.completion: nohup is not a service manager. It provides limited detachment, not supervision, restart policy, or structured logs.

lessons.title: Start with adjusted scheduling priority
lessons.about: nice starts a command with an adjusted niceness value. Higher niceness generally means lower CPU scheduling priority.
lessons.task: Run true with niceness 5.
hints: Use nice -n 5 followed by true.
lessons.completion: Niceness influences CPU scheduling; it is not a hard resource limit or a guarantee of runtime share.

lessons.title: Bound command runtime
lessons.about: timeout runs a command with a deadline and sends a signal if the duration is exceeded. Its exit status distinguishes a timeout from ordinary success.
lessons.task: Limit sleep 5 to one second.
hints: Put the one-second limit before the sleep command.
lessons.completion: A timeout bounds waiting; it does not prove the child and every descendant cleaned up all external state.

lessons.title: Pause for a bounded duration
lessons.about: sleep delays for a specified duration. Fractional seconds are supported by GNU sleep.
lessons.task: Pause for one tenth of a second.
hints: Use a fractional duration of 0.1.
lessons.completion: Sleep-based synchronization is fragile. Prefer an observable readiness condition when coordinating real work.

lessons.title: Measure one command execution
lessons.about: Bash time reports elapsed, user CPU, and system CPU time for a pipeline. -p uses a portable output shape.
breakdown: Timing data is written to stderr by the shell.
lessons.task: Measure sleep 0.1 with portable time output.
hints: Use Bash time -p before sleep.

checks.description: Portable timing output includes real time.

lessons.completion: One timing sample includes scheduler and system noise. Repeat controlled measurements before drawing performance conclusions.

lessons.title: Generate a numeric sequence
lessons.about: seq prints numeric sequences with optional start, increment, and end values. It is useful for bounded loops and generated test input.
breakdown: One argument is the final value.
The default start and increment are both one.
lessons.task: Print integers 3 through 7, inclusive.
hints: Provide start 3 and end 7.
lessons.completion: Keep generated ranges bounded. An accidental huge sequence can consume time, storage, or downstream resources.

lessons.title: Identify the kernel family
lessons.about: uname reports kernel and machine facts. -s selects only the kernel name.
breakdown: The result is Linux on the supported platform.
lessons.task: Print only the kernel name.
hints: Use the kernel-name option.

checks.description: The Linux kernel name was printed.

lessons.completion: Kernel name, distribution, release, and architecture are different facts. Ask for each explicitly.

lessons.title: Read the current host name
lessons.about: hostname prints or, with privilege and options, can change the system host name. This rep performs a read only.
breakdown: No option requests the current configured hostname.
The value depends on the environment.
lessons.task: Print the current hostname.
hints: Run hostname without options.
lessons.completion: A hostname is an administrative label, not proof of identity, DNS registration, or network reachability.

lessons.title: Read uptime and load averages
lessons.about: uptime reports current time, time since boot, user count, and load averages. Load average is not CPU percentage.
breakdown: The three loads cover different averaging windows.
lessons.task: Print the current system uptime summary.
hints: No option is required.
lessons.completion: Interpret load relative to runnable work, CPU count, and I/O conditions; it is not a standalone health score.

lessons.title: Format a fixed timestamp
lessons.about: date displays and formats time. GNU date -d can parse an explicit input, making transformations deterministic.
lessons.task: Print Unix epoch zero as a UTC YYYY-MM-DD date.
hints: Use UTC, input @0, and format %F.
lessons.completion: Always state timezone and input interpretation when timestamps become evidence or cross-system data.

lessons.title: Print a calendar
lessons.about: cal prints calendars for a month or year. It is commonly provided by the ncal package rather than coreutils.
lessons.task: Print the calendar for January 2000.
hints: Provide month number 1 and year 2000.
lessons.completion: Calendar layout and week conventions can be locale-dependent. Do not parse the human display as a data format.

lessons.title: Run with a controlled environment
lessons.about: env prints variables or runs a command with selected environment assignments. -i starts from an empty environment.
breakdown: printenv reads it in the child.
lessons.task: Run printenv with an otherwise empty environment containing MODE=practice, and print MODE.
hints: Use env -i, add the assignment, then run printenv.

checks.description: The controlled MODE value was printed.

lessons.completion: Environment variables influence child processes. Record relevant variables when reproducing context-dependent behavior.

lessons.title: Read one environment variable
lessons.about: printenv prints environment variables visible to the process. Naming one variable avoids dumping unrelated or sensitive values.
breakdown: HOME is the requested variable name.
Only its current value is printed.
lessons.task: Print only the HOME value supplied to this disposable rep.
hints: Name HOME explicitly instead of dumping the entire environment.

checks.description: The isolated HOME value was printed.

lessons.completion: Environment dumps can contain secrets. Query only the variable needed and handle output accordingly.

lessons.title: Inspect filesystem capacity
lessons.about: df reports filesystem-level space. -P requests a predictable POSIX-style row layout for simple inspection.
lessons.example_output: Filesystem 1024-blocks Used Available Capacity Mounted on
breakdown: . selects the filesystem containing the current directory.
lessons.task: Print the POSIX-style filesystem capacity row for the current workspace.
hints: Use -P and select the current directory.
lessons.completion: df reports filesystem capacity; du reports space attributed to paths. They answer different questions.

lessons.title: Measure path disk usage
lessons.about: du walks paths and reports allocated disk usage. -s summarizes and -k reports KiB units.
lessons.task: Print one KiB summary for the data directory.
hints: Combine summary and KiB options.

checks.description: A numeric KiB count and data label were printed.

lessons.completion: Allocated size can differ from apparent byte size because of blocks, sparse files, compression, and deduplication.

lessons.title: Inspect memory accounting
lessons.about: free summarizes memory and swap from kernel accounting. -h selects human-readable units.
breakdown: available is usually more useful than treating cache as simply used.
lessons.task: Print human-readable memory accounting.
hints: Use the human-readable option.

checks.description: The memory summary includes a Mem row.

lessons.completion: Linux uses memory for cache and can reclaim it. Interpret available memory and workload behavior, not one used number alone.

lessons.title: Create an archive
lessons.about: tar stores multiple paths and metadata in one archive. -c creates, -f names the archive, and -z adds gzip compression.
lessons.task: Create evidence.tar.gz containing the evidence directory.
hints: Use create, gzip, and file options together.
lessons.completion: An archive groups paths; compression reduces some data. List and test an archive before deleting sources.

lessons.title: Compress one file with gzip
lessons.about: gzip compresses individual files and normally replaces the source with a .gz file.
breakdown: The default result is report.txt.gz and the source name is removed.
lessons.task: Compress report.txt with gzip.
hints: Pass the source filename directly to gzip.

checks.description: The default gzip operation removed report.txt.

lessons.completion: Use gzip -k when the original file must remain. Compression is not encryption or integrity authentication.

lessons.title: Restore gzip-compressed content
lessons.about: gunzip expands .gz data. This rep creates a synthetic compressed input, then restores it in the disposable workspace.
breakdown: gunzip restores note.txt after successful compression.
lessons.task: Compress data.txt and then restore it with gunzip.
hints: Create data.txt.gz first, then run gunzip only after success.

checks.description: The default gunzip operation removed data.txt.gz.

lessons.completion: Decompression can overwrite or create paths. Inspect archive provenance and destination boundaries before extracting untrusted data.

lessons.title: Compress with bzip2
lessons.about: bzip2 compresses files using the Burrows-Wheeler family of transforms and normally replaces the source with .bz2.
lessons.task: Compress report.txt with bzip2.
hints: Pass the source directly to bzip2.
lessons.completion: Compression formats trade speed, size, and compatibility. Choose based on the consumer and verify the result.

lessons.title: Restore bzip2-compressed content
lessons.about: bunzip2 expands .bz2 files. The default removes the compressed input after successful restoration.
lessons.task: Compress data.txt and restore it with bunzip2.
hints: Create the .bz2 input before invoking bunzip2.
lessons.completion: Test restoration before treating a compressed file as a sufficient backup.

lessons.title: Compress with xz
lessons.about: xz compresses files using the LZMA2 format and normally replaces the source with .xz.
lessons.task: Compress report.txt with xz.
hints: Pass the source filename to xz.
lessons.completion: xz often favors compression ratio over speed. The best choice depends on data, time, memory, and compatibility.

lessons.title: Restore xz-compressed content
lessons.about: unxz expands .xz files and normally removes the compressed input after success.
lessons.task: Compress data.txt and restore it with unxz.
hints: Create the .xz input first, then restore it.
lessons.completion: Successful decompression is an observable check; add a trusted digest when exact integrity matters.

lessons.title: Create a ZIP archive
lessons.about: zip creates a broadly compatible archive that can contain multiple files. -q suppresses progress noise in this rep.
breakdown: The two source files remain in place.
lessons.task: Create bundle.zip containing one.txt and two.txt.
hints: Name the archive before the source files.
lessons.completion: ZIP paths can overwrite files when extracted. Inspect names and extract untrusted archives into a disposable directory.

lessons.title: Extract a ZIP archive
lessons.about: unzip lists or extracts ZIP archives. This rep creates a synthetic archive, removes the source, and restores it in disposable state.
lessons.example: zip -q bundle.zip note.txt && rm note.txt && unzip -q bundle.zip
breakdown: unzip restores it after both earlier steps succeed.
lessons.task: Archive note.txt, remove the original, and restore it with unzip.
lessons.solution: zip -q bundle.zip note.txt && rm note.txt && unzip -q bundle.zip
hints: Chain zip, rm, and unzip with &&.

checks.description: note.txt was restored from the archive.

lessons.completion: Use unzip -l to inspect names first and extract unknown archives inside a controlled destination.

lessons.title: Calculate an exact SHA-256 digest
lessons.about: sha256sum hashes exact file bytes. A digest supports equality and integrity comparisons when the expected value is trusted.
breakdown: The digest and filename are printed.
lessons.task: Calculate the SHA-256 digest of artifact.txt.
hints: Pass the filename directly to sha256sum.

checks.description: The exact digest and filename were printed.

lessons.completion: A hash says nothing about authorship or safety unless the expected digest comes from a trusted channel.

lessons.title: Inspect network interfaces
lessons.about: ip is the modern Linux interface for addresses, links, routes, and neighbors. -brief gives a compact human-readable summary.
lessons.task: Print a brief summary of interface addresses.
hints: Use ip brief mode with the address object.

checks.description: The loopback interface appears in the address summary.

lessons.completion: An assigned address does not prove routing, DNS, firewall permission, or application reachability.

lessons.title: Inspect listening TCP sockets
lessons.about: ss reports socket state from the kernel. -l selects listening sockets, -n avoids name resolution, and -t selects TCP.
lessons.example_output: State Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port Peer Address:Port
lessons.task: Print listening TCP sockets with numeric addresses and ports.
hints: Combine listener, numeric, and TCP options.

checks.description: The socket table header was printed.

lessons.completion: A listener proves a local socket state, not that a remote client can reach or successfully use the service.

lessons.title: Test local ICMP echo
lessons.about: ping sends ICMP echo requests and measures responses. This rep targets loopback only, requiring no external network.
lessons.task: Send one ICMP echo request to IPv4 loopback.
hints: Use count 1 and target 127.0.0.1.

checks.description: One response was received from loopback.

lessons.completion: Ping success proves ICMP echo for one target and moment. Ping failure does not identify the failed network layer by itself.

lessons.title: Read a local URL
lessons.about: curl transfers data using URL schemes. This rep uses a file URL inside the disposable workspace, so no network request leaves the machine.
breakdown: file:// reads a local path rather than making a network request.
lessons.task: Use curl silently to print message.txt through a file URL rooted at $PWD.
hints: Use the file:// scheme and the PWD environment variable.
lessons.completion: For HTTP work, record method, URL, status, headers, and body deliberately. Silent mode can hide useful diagnostics.

lessons.title: Inspect the installed wget version
lessons.about: wget is a noninteractive network downloader. To keep this core rep offline, it inspects the local version rather than contacting a remote host.
lessons.task: Print only the first line of wget version information.
hints: Request version output and bound it with head.

checks.description: The GNU Wget version line was printed.

lessons.completion: Before downloading, decide the destination, overwrite behavior, redirects, trust source, and integrity check.

lessons.title: Inspect effective SSH client configuration
lessons.about: ssh -G prints the client configuration that would apply to a host without making a connection.
breakdown: grep selects the effective port line.
lessons.task: Print the effective SSH port for host example.invalid without connecting.
hints: Use ssh configuration mode -G, then select the port line.

checks.description: The effective default SSH port was printed.

lessons.completion: ssh -G is excellent for debugging config precedence. A resolved configuration does not prove network reachability or authentication.

lessons.title: Use scp's local copy form
lessons.about: scp copies files using SSH when a path includes a remote host. With two local paths, it performs a local copy, which keeps this rep offline.
breakdown: The data stays inside the disposable workspace.
lessons.task: Copy artifact.txt to staged.txt using scp without a remote host.
hints: Use two plain local paths; do not add a colon or host.
lessons.completion: Real remote scp adds host-key verification, authentication, network, destination-permission, and integrity considerations.

lessons.title: Synchronize local directory content
lessons.about: rsync copies differences efficiently and can preserve selected metadata. A trailing slash changes whether the source directory itself or its contents are copied.
breakdown: source/ with a trailing slash means copy its contents.
lessons.task: Synchronize the contents of source/ into destination/ with archive mode.
hints: Use -a and keep the trailing slash on source/.
lessons.completion: rsync --delete and trailing-slash mistakes can remove or reshape data. Dry-run broad synchronization changes first.

lessons.title: Identify the installed systemd manager
lessons.about: systemctl controls and queries systemd units. This safe core rep prints version information and does not change a unit.
lessons.task: Print only the first line of systemctl version information.
hints: Use --version and head.

checks.description: A systemd version line was printed.

lessons.completion: systemctl is systemd-specific. Other Linux distributions or containers may use a different init/service model.

lessons.title: Identify the systemd journal client
lessons.about: journalctl queries systemd's journal. This core rep prints local version information without requiring journal access or changing state.
lessons.task: Print only the first line of journalctl version information.
hints: Use --version and keep the first line.

checks.description: A systemd version line was printed.

lessons.completion: Journal availability depends on systemd, permissions, retention, namespaces, and persistent-storage configuration.
